slides.title: Chapter 4: Keys and Addresses

items.cap: Figure 4-2, Mastering Bitcoin 3rd edition, CC BY-SA 4.0

slides.notes: Chapter 3 showed the software that checks the rules; this chapter opens the smallest secret it protects. Point at the three ovals: a number becomes a point, and the point becomes a string you can read aloud. Ask who has ever typed a Bitcoin address by hand. Every result in this deck was computed by the chapter library.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.take: Five parts, three true stories, twenty-one examples
slides.notes: The route has five parts around one key, and the tiles at the right count slides, true stories and code examples. Point at the ranges and tell students each one is a jump target. Ask them to hold one question per part. A common mistake is to skip the first part because it looks like mathematics.

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers

items: What is a private key, and what makes one safe to use?
How does a private key become a public key, and why can it not be reversed?
How does a public key become a legacy address, and why does it carry a checksum?
What do P2SH, Bech32 and Bech32m change about addresses?
How is a private key written down so that a wallet can import it?
Why can an address be valid and still have no key behind it?

slides.notes: Read the six questions aloud and promise to return to them in the summary. Ask which one a student can already half-answer. The fourth question, about P2SH, Bech32 and Bech32m, usually draws the most guesses. A common mistake is to treat the sixth question as a trick; it has a real answer on the last story.

slides.title: The chapter in one picture
slides.take: Random bits, a key, a point, a hash, an address
slides.notes: This picture is the skeleton of the lecture: entropy, private key, public key, hash, address. Point at the arrows and say that each one runs forward easily and backwards never. Ask where a thief could break in if one arrow could be reversed. A common mistake is to think the address contains the public key.

slides.title: Public Key Cryptography
slides.sub: From one secret number to a point that nobody can run backwards

items.meaning: A secret 256-bit number; whoever knows it can spend the coins.
items.analogy: Think of the one key to your front door.

items.meaning: A point on the curve computed from the private key; safe to publish.
items.analogy: Think of the lock on your door: everyone can see it.

items.meaning: The curve y squared equals x cubed plus 7 that Bitcoin uses.
items.analogy: Think of the one game board that every player agrees on.

slides.notes: Part 1 asks what a key is. Point at the three tiles: a secret number, a point computed from it, and the one curve everybody shares. Read each everyday picture aloud and ask which one a student could explain to a friend. A common mistake is to call the public key a second secret.

slides.title: Keys: concepts (1 of 2)
slides.take: Think of each row as a flashcard: the concept, then a picture you know
slides.notes: These rows pair each concept with something familiar. Say the meaning first, then the comparison, in your own words. Ask students to cover the right column and supply their own picture. A common mistake is to memorise the pictures and forget what they stand for.

slides.title: Keys: concepts (2 of 2)
slides.take: Think of each row as a flashcard: the concept, then a picture you know
slides.notes: The second half of the concept table covers the curve and doubling. Point at the rows about the generator and the one-way idea. Ask which picture would not work for a non-technical friend. A common mistake is to think the curve is drawn as a smooth line on the real numbers in Bitcoin; it is a scatter of points.

slides.title: The 1976 paper that split the key in two
slides.sub: 3 June 1976 · public-key cryptography is born

items.cap: Picture: Whitfield Diffie, 2017 - Duncan Hull, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

items.who: Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman, the Stanford researchers who wrote the paper and received the Turing Award for it
items.where: IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, volume IT-22, number 6

slides.take: Every address in this chapter stands on one 1976 idea
slides.notes: Tell the story slowly: Diffie and Hellman, Stanford, 3 June 1976, a key split in two. Point at the photograph and the link to the paper; ask what problem a publishable half solves. It removes the need to carry secrets to every partner. A common mistake is to think the paper describes Bitcoin; it describes the idea Bitcoin uses.

slides.title: A digital signature proves you hold the key
slides.sub: Sign with the private key, verify with the public key
slides.notes: A digital signature is a pair of numbers made from a message and a private key. Point at the three checks: the real message passes, a changed message and a wrong key fail. Ask why the hash changes in 135 of 256 bits after a one-digit edit. A common mistake is to think the signature hides the message.
slides.take: Only the key holder can sign; anyone can verify

slides.title: A lambda is a function without a name
slides.sub: The one-line helper that the next code uses
slides.notes: A lambda is a function without a name. Point at the four tiles: the keyword, the input, the colon and the returned value, then at the same helper written with def. Ask what ok(0) gives; false; three later code boxes use it. A common mistake is to think the name ok belongs to the function.
slides.take: A lambda is a tiny function written where it is needed

slides.title: A private key is a number below n
slides.sub: The book's example key, and the edges of the range
slides.take: Any whole number from 1 to n minus 1 is a key
slides.notes: A private key is any whole number from 1 to n minus 1. Point at the five verdicts: zero and n fail, the rest pass. Ask how many valid keys exist; about 2 to the 256. A common mistake is to think a key must look random; the range is the only rule, randomness is a separate duty.

slides.title: Entropy: bits an attacker must guess
slides.sub: Why a Bitcoin key needs 256 fair coin flips
slides.take: Only truly random choices reach the 256 bits of a key
slides.notes: Entropy counts the bits a guesser must get right. Point at the chart: a PIN gives 13 bits, a long password 79, a key 256. Ask how many fair coin flips equal a key. A common mistake is to type a clever phrase and call it random; people choose far fewer bits than they think.

slides.title: Secure randomness decides how safe a key is
slides.sub: The secrets module for keys, random only for simulation
slides.notes: Keys need a source nobody can guess. Point at the table: secrets reads the system's secure source, random is a fast generator whose state can be recovered from 624 outputs. Ask which module a game uses and which one a wallet uses. A common mistake is to seed random with the clock and call it secure.
slides.take: If the source can be guessed, the key can be guessed

slides.title: The curve secp256k1 and its generator
slides.sub: Checking that G really lies on the curve
slides.take: The curve is one short formula: y squared = x cubed + 7
slides.notes: Bitcoin's curve is y squared equals x cubed plus 7, counted modulo a big prime. Point at the result: the generator G satisfies it, so the answer is True. Ask what G is for; every public key is a multiple of it. A common mistake is to forget the modulo and test with ordinary arithmetic.

slides.title: A finite field: arithmetic on a clock face
slides.sub: Why every coordinate stays inside 256 bits
slides.notes: A finite field is arithmetic that wraps around, like a clock. Point at the cell 3: thirteen plus seven is twenty, which wraps to 3. Ask what division by 5 means modulo 17; multiplying by 7. A common mistake is to use ordinary division, which would leave the whole numbers.
slides.take: Wrap around at p and every answer stays exact

slides.title: The curve secp256k1 and the curve standard
slides.sub: One curve, one generator, one agreed list of parameters
slides.notes: One curve and one standard make every wallet agree. Point at the parameters on the left and at the NIST column on the right: secp256k1 is in SEC 2 but not on the NIST list. Ask why agreement matters; different curves give different keys. A common mistake is to think secp256k1 is a NIST curve.
slides.take: A standard fixes the numbers so every program agrees

slides.title: Points on a curve: doubling G
slides.take: Tangent, meeting point, mirror image: that is one doubling
slides.notes: One doubling in three moves: tangent, meeting point, mirror. Point at the labels G, 2G, 4G and 8G on the figure. Ask what happens if the tangent is vertical; the result is the point at infinity. A common mistake is to read the picture as a proof that the same drawing works modulo a prime; it only gives the idea.

slides.title: Adding points, and the point at infinity
slides.sub: Line, third point, mirror: the rule behind k times G
slides.notes: Adding points is a line, a third point and a mirror. Point at the teal dots, the multiples of P, and at the last row: a point plus its mirror image gives infinity. Ask what infinity is for; it is zero. A common mistake is to add the coordinates like ordinary numbers.
slides.take: Adding points is the one step the whole chapter repeats

slides.title: Doubling and adding: k times G
slides.sub: How one multiplication reaches a huge number
slides.take: Doubling reaches a 256-bit key in a few hundred steps
slides.notes: Multiplying G by k means adding G to itself k times, and doubling makes it fast. Point at the count: 252 doublings and 123 additions for the book's key. Ask why that beats 10 to the 76 additions. A common mistake is to think the computer loops k times.

slides.title: The point at infinity on a toy curve
slides.sub: A curve over 17 numbers, small enough to list
slides.take: Multiples of a point repeat; the cycle closes at infinity
slides.notes: On a toy curve with 17 numbers we can list every multiple. Point at the ninth row: None, the point at infinity, and then the list repeats. Ask what a cycle means for the size of a group. A common mistake is to treat None as an error; it is the zero of the curve.

slides.title: One-way: the work to find a key
slides.sub: Why the public key cannot be run backwards
slides.take: Each extra bit doubles the attacker's work
slides.notes: Finding k from kG means trying keys one by one. Point at the chart: 6, 12, 24, 38 and 77 are powers of ten, so a 20-bit key falls quickly and a 256-bit key never does. Ask why each extra bit doubles the work. A common mistake is to read the chart as bits instead of powers of ten.

slides.title: Why the multiplier cannot be found
slides.sub: The discrete logarithm problem and brute-force search
slides.notes: The discrete logarithm is the hard direction. Point at the nine tries on the toy group and then at the secp256k1 row: about 1.8 times 10 to the 57 years at a trillion tries a second. Ask why nobody can use a faster computer. A common mistake is to think the problem is merely slow instead of out of reach.
slides.take: Going forward is quick; going back is a search through half of all keys

slides.title: Do not write your own cryptography
slides.sub: A readable sketch next to a tested library
slides.notes: Write the sketch to learn and use a library to protect money. Point at the bars: the sketch does more work for a key with more 1-bits, so its timing leaks. Ask what constant-time means; the same time for every key. A common mistake is to copy teaching code into a real wallet.
slides.take: Use a tested library for anything that guards real money

slides.title: Legacy Addresses
slides.sub: From a public key to the address that people read aloud

items.meaning: Pay to public key hash: the output script holds only a 20-byte hash.
items.analogy: Think of a locker that shows a number, never the shape of the key.

items.meaning: SHA256 followed by RIPEMD-160: the 20-byte hash of a public key.
items.analogy: Think of two sieves in a row: the finer one decides.

items.meaning: Version byte, payload and checksum written in base58.
items.analogy: Think of a parcel with a label, a content and a seal.

slides.notes: Part 2 turns a public key into the first kind of address. Point at the three tiles: a locker that shows a number, two sieves in a row, and a labelled parcel. Ask what the hash hides; the key itself, until spending. A common mistake is to think the address is the public key in another alphabet.

slides.title: Legacy: concepts (1 of 3)
slides.take: Think of each row as a flashcard: the concept, then a picture you know
slides.notes: Legacy concepts, first page. Say each meaning, then the picture. Ask which row explains why an address is shorter than a key. A common mistake is to confuse a script with an address; the script is the lock, the address is its printed label.

slides.title: Legacy: concepts (2 of 3)
slides.take: Think of each row as a flashcard: the concept, then a picture you know
slides.notes: Legacy concepts, second page. Point at the rows on Base58Check and the checksum; ask what a checksum adds. It lets a wallet notice a typo before any money moves. A common mistake is to think a checksum hides or protects anything; it only detects mistakes.

slides.title: Legacy: concepts (3 of 3)
slides.take: Think of each row as a flashcard: the concept, then a picture you know
slides.notes: Legacy concepts, last page. Point at the rows on compressed keys and the hash commitment. Ask why two forms of one key give two addresses. A common mistake is to treat the compressed flag as a smaller private key; the private key never changes.

slides.title: Bits, bytes and number bases
slides.sub: The same public key written in four ways
slides.notes: The same key, four ways; point at the bars: 264 binary characters, 66 hex, 44 in base64, 45 in base58. Ask why base58 is not shorter than base64. It drops look-alike characters, trading length for readability. A common mistake is to confuse the number of bits with the number of characters.
slides.take: A larger base writes the same number in fewer characters

slides.title: The first way to pay: an IP address
slides.sub: Why Bitcoin moved to addresses
slides.notes: The first payments went to an IP address. Point at the four steps and at the receiver lane: it had to be online and reachable. Ask what could go wrong if someone else answered; nothing proved who they were. A common mistake is to think an address replaced the key; it replaced this handshake.
slides.take: An address lets anyone pay you while you are offline

slides.title: A public key has two encodings
slides.sub: Compressed keys keep x and the parity of y
slides.take: A compressed key is 33 bytes; the full one is 65
slides.notes: A public key has two encodings; point at the lengths: 33 bytes compressed, 65 uncompressed, and the first byte 3 or 4. Ask what the first byte tells a reader. Compression keeps x and the parity of y, and decompressing returns the same point. A common mistake is to think compressed keys are weaker.

slides.title: P2PK holds the key, P2PKH only its hash
slides.sub: Two output scripts for the same public key
slides.take: P2PKH shows a commitment to the key, not the key
slides.notes: P2PK holds the key, P2PKH only a hash of it. Point at the sizes 35 and 25 bytes and at the shared last byte, ac, the signature check. Ask what the shorter script hides; the key stays secret until the coins move. A common mistake is to call P2PKH an address; it is the script behind one.

slides.title: Scripts run on a stack
slides.sub: A P2PKH script, one opcode at a time
slides.notes: Scripts run on a stack. Point at the right-hand chip in each row, the top of the stack, and follow it from the unlocking data to true. Ask what OP_EQUALVERIFY removes; the two equal hashes. A common mistake is to think the script runs a loop; it is a straight line of steps.
slides.take: Each opcode takes the top items and pushes its result

slides.title: HASH160 is SHA256 then RIPEMD-160
slides.sub: Two hashes turn a 33-byte key into 20 bytes
slides.take: Two hashes in a row: 33 bytes in, 20 bytes out
slides.notes: HASH160 is SHA256 followed by RIPEMD-160. Point at the chart: 33 bytes in, 32 after the first hash, 20 after the second. Ask why two different hashes are used. A common mistake is to think the result is 32 bytes or to hash in the other order.

slides.title: A hash is a commitment to a key
slides.sub: Publish the hash now, reveal the key when spending
slides.notes: A hash commits to a key without showing it. Point at the table: the real key matches, one flipped bit does not, and 78 of 160 hash bits change. Ask why a near-miss is no help to a forger; the whole hash changes. A common mistake is to think the hash can be reversed to the key.
slides.take: The address commits to the key without showing it

slides.title: Why 58? Satoshi left the reasons in the file
slides.sub: 8 January 2009 · a design memo inside base58.h

items.cap: Picture: Satoshi bust, Budapest - Fekist, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons - a stand-in, since the author's face is unknown

items.who: Satoshi Nakamoto, named by the file's own copyright line
items.where: src/base58.h in the bitcoin/bitcoin source tree

slides.take: Address formats are human-factors engineering, written into the source
slides.notes: Tell the story: Satoshi's design memo in base58.h, with four human reasons. Point at the bust and at the link to the file. Ask which reason matters most when you read an address aloud over the phone. A common mistake is to think the alphabet was chosen for mathematics.

slides.title: Base58Check, step by step
slides.sub: Version, hash and checksum become an address
slides.take: An address is 25 bytes written in 34 characters
slides.notes: A legacy address has three parts: version byte, 20-byte hash, four checksum bytes. Point at the second code box where the checksum is cut from a double SHA256. Ask how long the result is: 25 bytes become 34 characters starting with 1. A common mistake is to forget the version byte.

slides.title: From public key to address
slides.take: Each arrow is a function that you have just run
slides.notes: Figure 4-7 is the whole road in one picture. Point at the boxes and the sizes beside them: 33, 32, 20, 25 bytes and 34 characters. Ask which arrow cannot be reversed; all of them can be computed forward only. A common mistake is to read the figure as a recipe you could run backwards.

slides.title: The P2PKH address and its script
slides.sub: One lock and its printed label
slides.notes: A P2PKH address is a label for a 25-byte script. Point at the two strips: the script holds the hash between OP_HASH160 and OP_EQUALVERIFY, the address holds version, hash and checksum. Ask why there are two addresses for one key; compressed and uncompressed hash differently. A common mistake is to mix the script and the address.
slides.take: The address is a short label for the 25-byte script

slides.title: The checksum catches every single typo
slides.sub: Every one-character mistake, tried one by one
slides.take: A single typo is caught almost every time
slides.notes: We change one character of the address in every possible way, 1,938 variants. Point at the result: none is accepted. Ask why the check still fails once in 4,294,967,296 random tries; four checksum bytes give 32 bits. A common mistake is to think the checksum can fix the typo; it can only reject it.

slides.title: Mainnet and testnet look different on purpose
slides.sub: Version bytes and human-readable parts keep the chains apart
slides.notes: The network is written into the address. Point at the version bytes 00 and 6F and at bc against tb. Ask what a wallet does with a tb1 address when set to the main network; it refuses. A common mistake is to think test coins have value or that the two chains share data.
slides.take: An address tells a wallet which chain it belongs to

slides.title: Script Hashes and Bech32
slides.sub: Addresses that commit to a script, and the second alphabet

items.meaning: Pay to script hash: spending reveals the script and then satisfies it.
items.analogy: Think of a locked briefcase opened in front of the cashier.

items.meaning: SegWit addresses in lowercase letters and digits with a stronger checksum.
items.analogy: Think of a postcode that also detects a mistyped letter.

items.meaning: The same encoding with a new checksum constant, used from witness version 1.
items.analogy: Think of a corrected second edition of the same form.

slides.notes: Part 3 covers what came after the first address. Point at the three tiles: a script hash, SegWit's Bech32 and its corrected twin. Ask what the postcode picture means for a mistyped letter. A common mistake is to think Bech32m is a different address kind rather than a repaired checksum.

slides.title: Bech32: concepts (1 of 2)
slides.take: Think of each row as a flashcard: the concept, then a picture you know
slides.notes: Concepts of script hashes and Bech32, first page. Say the meaning, then the picture. Ask which row would let a company require two signatures. A common mistake is to think a P2SH address reveals its script; it commits to it.

slides.title: Bech32: concepts (2 of 2)
slides.take: Think of each row as a flashcard: the concept, then a picture you know
slides.notes: Concepts of script hashes and Bech32, second page. Point at the rows on witness version and human-readable part. Ask what the part before the 1 is for; it names the network. A common mistake is to read the 1 as part of the data; it is the separator.

slides.title: Multisignature: any two of three keys
slides.sub: OP_CHECKMULTISIG in a 105-byte script
slides.notes: Multisignature means m of n keys. Point at the eight boxes: only the four with at least two signers pass. Ask who can spend if one key is lost; the other two together. A common mistake is to think the script lists the signers; it lists the keys and a count.
slides.take: Several keys share control; no single key decides alone

slides.title: P2SH commits to a whole script
slides.sub: A two-of-three multisignature behind one address
slides.take: A P2SH address hides the script until spending
slides.notes: A P2SH address stands for any script. Point at the two-of-three redeem script of 105 bytes and at the address starting with 3. Ask what the spender must reveal; all 105 bytes, then satisfy them. A common mistake is to think the address contains the keys.

slides.title: Collision and preimage: bits of work
slides.sub: Why a 160-bit hash is weaker for scripts
slides.take: A collision costs only half the bits of a hash
slides.notes: Two lambdas give the work in bits for two attacks. Point at the 80 and 128 against 160 and 256: collisions are far cheaper than preimages. Ask which attack matters for an address you created yourself. A common mistake is to read the chart as seconds instead of bits.

slides.title: Second preimage: matching a given hash
slides.sub: Three attacks and the work each one needs
slides.notes: Three attacks, three amounts of work. Point at the bars on the power-of-two scale: collisions need 2 to the 80, the two preimage attacks 2 to the 160. Ask why a second preimage attack matters for your own address. It would let someone spend with another key; a common mistake is to confuse it with a collision.
slides.take: Matching a given hash is as hard as 2 to the 160 tries

slides.title: Segregated witness separates the signatures
slides.sub: Why the transaction identifier stops changing
slides.notes: Segregated witness moves the signatures out of the transaction identifier. Point at the orange block: before it sits inside the hash, after it travels alone. Ask who could change the identifier before; a third party who re-encoded the signature. A common mistake is to think the signatures disappear; they move.
slides.take: Signatures leave the identifier, so nobody can alter it

slides.title: Segwit inside P2SH: a bridge for old wallets
slides.sub: A witness program wrapped in a script hash
slides.notes: Segwit inside P2SH is a bridge. Point at the redeem script of 22 bytes and at the 3 address that holds it. Ask why an old wallet can pay it; it only needs to know P2SH. A common mistake is to think the address is shorter; it has 34 characters, like P2PKH.
slides.take: An old payer can pay a new receiver without knowing it

slides.title: A Bech32 address, taken apart
slides.sub: Network, version, program and checksum
slides.take: Split at the last 1: name, version, program, checksum
slides.notes: A Bech32 address has four parts: network name, separator, data, six checksum letters. Point at the result: bc, q, 32 program letters and c6aaee. Ask what the first data letter says; it is the witness version. A common mistake is to split at the first 1 instead of the last.

slides.title: Bech32 catches typing mistakes
slides.sub: A BCH code with a guarantee
slides.notes: Bech32 uses a BCH code, not a plain checksum. Point at the table: every one of 1,209 single-letter errors and every sampled two- and four-letter error is caught. Ask what happens with five; about one in a billion slips through. A common mistake is to think the code corrects errors; here it detects them.
slides.take: Any error in four letters or fewer is always caught

slides.title: Witness version and witness program
slides.sub: Three addresses from the book, decoded
slides.take: Version 0 for older SegWit; version 1 for Taproot
slides.notes: The decoder returns the version and the program. Point at the three rows: version 0 with 20 or 32 bytes, version 1 with 32 bytes. Ask which letter changes for version 1; it changes from q to p. A common mistake is to assume every program is 20 bytes.

slides.title: Three segwit output types
slides.sub: Key hash, script hash and Taproot key
slides.notes: Three segwit output types share one shape. Point at each strip: a version byte, a push and a program of 20 or 32 bytes. Ask which one commits to a script; p2WSH. A common mistake is to assume P2TR is a hash; its program is a point on the curve.
slides.take: All three are a version, a push and a program

slides.title: Bech32 accepts the extra q, Bech32m does not
slides.sub: The weakness that Bech32m repaired
slides.take: Bech32m changed one constant and closed the gap
slides.notes: A lambda tests an address against a checksum constant. Point at the first list, all True, and the second, all False. Ask why the old check cannot see the extra q; that is the length-extension weakness. A common mistake is to think Bech32m forbids the strings; it simply gives them a different checksum.

slides.title: The weakness that bech32m repairs
slides.sub: A letter q before the final p
slides.notes: The weakness is quiet. Point at the orange q letters before the final p: every string is valid under Bech32 and none under Bech32m. Ask what a user would see; nothing wrong. A common mistake is to think a longer address is a different address; the checksum cannot tell them apart.
slides.take: In bech32 one q more or less goes unnoticed

slides.title: Bech32m changes one constant
slides.sub: Which checksum constant goes with which witness version
slides.notes: Bech32m changes only one constant. Point at the switch on the left and at the table: version 0 addresses verify with 1, the Taproot address with 0x2bc830a3. Ask which constant a version 1 address needs; the second. A common mistake is to use Bech32m for version 0.
slides.take: Version 0 uses bech32; versions 1 and later use bech32m

slides.title: Capitals make smaller QR codes
slides.sub: The alphanumeric mode of a QR code
slides.notes: Capitals make smaller QR codes. Point at the two bars: 336 bits in byte mode, 231 in alphanumeric mode. Ask why base58 cannot do the same; it needs lowercase letters. A common mistake is to think a smaller picture changes the address; it is the same text in capitals.
slides.take: A bech32 address in capitals needs fewer bits

slides.title: Private Key Formats
slides.sub: The same private key, written in the forms a wallet can import

items.meaning: Wallet import format: Base58Check of a version byte 80 and the key.
items.analogy: Think of a key packed in a labelled travel case.

items.meaning: WIF with a final 01 byte that marks the key as compressed.
items.analogy: Think of a luggage tag that says travel light.

items.meaning: Not a smaller key: a flag that tells a wallet to use compressed public keys.
items.analogy: Think of a note that says use the short form of my name.

slides.notes: Part 4 is about writing a private key down. Point at the three tiles: WIF, WIF-compressed, and the compressed flag. Ask which one changes the address; the flag does, because it picks the public key form. A common mistake is to think a compressed private key is shorter by half.

slides.title: Formats: concepts
slides.take: Think of each row as a flashcard: the concept, then a picture you know
slides.notes: Key format concepts. Say the meaning, then the picture. Ask why a luggage tag is a fair picture for the final 01 byte. A common mistake is to believe the flag changes the number; it only tells the wallet which public key to use.

slides.title: WIF: a private key dressed for travel
slides.sub: Base58Check of version 80, the key and a flag
slides.take: The final 01 byte says: use compressed public keys
slides.notes: WIF wraps the key in Base58Check with version 80. Point at the two results: starts with 5 and 51 characters, or starts with K or L and 52 characters. Ask what the last byte 01 means; use the compressed public key. A common mistake is to confuse WIF with the address.

slides.title: One private key, two addresses
slides.sub: Compressed and uncompressed keys hash differently
slides.take: The flag in WIF decides which address a wallet watches
slides.notes: One private key, two public key forms, two addresses. Point at the prefixes 1424C2 and 1J7mdg. Ask where coins sent to the wrong one appear; they do not appear in the other. A common mistake is to import a key without keeping its compressed flag.

slides.title: Advanced Keys and Addresses
slides.sub: Chosen prefixes, printed keys and an address with no key

items.meaning: A vanity address starts with chosen letters, found by trying many keys.
items.analogy: Think of a custom number plate you must keep applying for.

items.meaning: A key and its address printed on paper and kept offline.
items.analogy: Think of a banknote locked in a drawer.

items.meaning: A hash that fixes a value now and lets you reveal it later.
items.analogy: Think of a sealed envelope holding your prediction.

slides.notes: Part 5 goes beyond a plain random key. Point at the three tiles: vanity addresses, paper wallets and the hash commitment. Ask which one costs electricity and which one costs care. A common mistake is to treat a vanity address as a different kind of address; it is a search.

slides.title: Advanced: concepts
slides.take: Think of each row as a flashcard: the concept, then a picture you know
slides.notes: Concepts of advanced keys. Say each meaning, then the picture. Ask why a sealed envelope is a good picture for a commitment. A common mistake is to think a paper wallet is safer by itself; today it is called obsolete.

slides.title: Vanity search: 58 times harder per letter
slides.sub: Trying keys until the address starts as chosen
slides.take: Every extra letter costs about 58 times more work
slides.notes: A vanity address is found by trying keys. Point at the chart: each extra letter costs 58 times more, six letters about 38 billion tries. Ask how many tries one letter took here; nineteen. A common mistake is to buy a vanity key from a stranger, who also knows the key.

slides.title: A paper wallet must give back its address
slides.sub: Print, scan and check before funding
slides.take: Test the paper before you put coins on it
slides.notes: A paper wallet prints a WIF key and its address. Point at the final line: the restored key reproduces the printed address, True. Ask what to do before funding it; test the round trip. A common mistake is to fund the address first and test later.

slides.title: Which address a wallet hands out by default
slides.sub: The four values of the addresstype option
slides.notes: The default is a policy. Point at the highlighted row: Bitcoin Core hands out bech32 unless the addresstype option says otherwise. Ask which value gives a Taproot address; bech32m. A common mistake is to think the default never changes; it follows what the ecosystem treats as current.
slides.take: Bitcoin Core hands out bech32 unless you ask otherwise

slides.title: Why a wallet no longer exports one key
slides.sub: dumpprivkey and importprivkey are gone
slides.notes: Exporting one key used to be routine. Point at the removed commands, dumpprivkey and importprivkey, and at the descriptor line that still accepts a WIF key. Ask why a single leaked key is dangerous in a deterministic wallet. It can reveal the others; a common mistake is to look for the old command in new releases.
slides.take: One exported key can endanger a whole deterministic wallet

slides.title: BIP38: a private key under a passphrase
slides.sub: Something you have plus something you know
slides.notes: BIP38 encrypts a key under a passphrase. Point at the 58-character record starting 6P and at the two factors, paper and passphrase. Ask why the status reads Deployed yet discouraged; it exists and is used, but reviewers advise against new support. A common mistake is to treat it as current practice.
slides.take: Encrypted keys are met on old paper wallets, not in new software

slides.title: One seed, every key
slides.sub: How a deterministic wallet derives its keys
slides.notes: One seed, every key. Point at the three keys, each the hash of the seed and a counter: 50b18e0b is the first. Ask what a backup must hold; only the seed. A common mistake is to think the book's hash trick is what real wallets use; it shows the idea, and the next chapter shows the real tree.
slides.take: Back up the seed once and every key comes back

slides.title: One address, one payment
slides.sub: Why reusing an address costs privacy
slides.notes: Reuse links payments; point at the left picture: one address, three payers, one story for an onlooker. On the right each payment has its own address. Ask who benefits from a link; anyone watching the chain. A common mistake is to think a new address needs a new backup; with a seed it does not.
slides.take: A fresh address for each payment keeps payments unlinked

slides.title: A hardware signing device keeps the key inside
slides.sub: The computer prepares, the device signs
slides.notes: The device keeps the key. Point at the box: the computer only prepares and broadcasts, the device shows and signs. Ask what an attacker on the computer sees; an unsigned transaction and a signed one, never the key. A common mistake is to think the device is a different kind of address.
slides.take: The key never meets general-purpose software

slides.title: The address that eats coins
slides.sub: 6 October 2026 · figures fetched from a block explorer

items.cap: Picture: Bitcoin logo - Grayliptrot, public domain, Wikimedia Commons - a stand-in, since an address has no picture

items.who: Blockstream Explorer, whose address page and API recorded the deposits of thousands of anonymous senders
items.where: the Bitcoin main chain, at address 1BitcoinEaterAddressDontSendf59kuE

slides.take: An address commits to a key; it does not prove that a key exists
slides.notes: Tell the story: a message spelled in base58, closed by a valid checksum, and thousands of deposits that can never move. Point at the explorer link. Ask who holds the key; nobody. A common mistake is to think a valid address means a key exists.

slides.title: The eater address is valid but keyless
slides.sub: A message spelled in base58, with a good checksum
slides.take: A valid checksum is not proof that a key exists
slides.notes: The address spells BitcoinEaterAddressDontSend and ends with f59kuE. Point at True: the checksum is correct, so wallets accept it silently. Ask what a checksum cannot check; whether anyone holds the key. A common mistake is to trust a green tick as proof of ownership.

slides.title: Test vectors and independent checks
slides.sub: How an implementation earns trust
slides.notes: Trust comes from agreement. Point at the vectors on the left: all eight valid addresses are accepted here, and the fifteen invalid ones are listed with reasons. On the right three independent sources give one address; ask why independence matters. A common mistake is to run only the examples that you expect to pass.
slides.take: Agreement between independent programs is the evidence

slides.title: A key proves control without a registry
slides.sub: Challenge, signature, check
slides.notes: Control is shown, not granted. Point at the three steps: a challenge, a signature, a check with the public key. Ask what the verifier needed; only the public key. A common mistake is to think the key holder must reveal the key; the signature is enough.
slides.take: Control is shown by signing, not by being on a list

slides.title: URIs and decentralized identifiers
slides.sub: A name for a thing, and a name you control with a key
slides.notes: A URI names a resource and a DID names a subject you control. Point at the three parts of each and at the DID document with a public key. Ask how a DID proves control; by a signature, as in this chapter. A common mistake is to think a DID needs a registry; its design avoids one.
slides.take: A DID is a URI whose controller proves control with a key

slides.title: Summary: the six answers
slides.take: Entropy, a point, a hash, a checksum, a flag, no key
slides.notes: Each row answers one of the six opening questions in a line. Point at the first words of each answer and ask students to answer in their own words, using the everyday pictures. A common mistake is to memorise the table instead of understanding one answer per question.

slides.notes: These links are all open and free. Point at the chapter source first, then the standards and the paper, then the eater address on the explorer. Ask which link a student will open tonight. The Computerphile video on elliptic curves is a good evening watch.

slides.title: Questions?

items: Next: chapter 5, Wallet Recovery: from a word list back to every key

slides.notes: That is the whole path from a secret number to an address. Chapter 5 asks what happens when the secret is lost, and how a word list brings every key back. Ask each student for one question and write them on the board for the next lecture.
